questions.title: Does the partition function $Z(x)$ actually vanish, or does it just become irrelevant?
questions.question_body:
I am reading the derivation in Section 3 where the authors substitute the reward parameterization back into the Bradley-Terry model. They state that 'the partition function cancels'. Looking at Equation 5, I see terms like $ eta  rac{1}{ eta}  eta  rac{1}{ eta}$... wait, looking closer at Equation 5:

$$p^*(y_1\succ y_2 \mid x)=\frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_2\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_2\mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi^*(y_1\mid x)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y_1\mid x)}\right)}$$

My confusion is: In Equation 4, $r(x,y)$ contains a $+ \beta \log Z(x)$ term. When calculating the difference $r(x, y_1) - r(x, y_2)$ inside the sigmoid function of the Bradley-Terry model (Equation 3), the $Z(x)$ terms subtract out ($Z(x) - Z(x) = 0$). Does this mean $Z(x)$ literally disappears from the math entirely? If so, why was it mentioned as a difficulty in Equation 4 earlier? Am I misunderstanding that 'cancels' means it is never calculated versus it being mathematically eliminated?

questions.title: Is DPO actually learning a reward model, or is it just doing supervised learning with a weird loss?
questions.question_body:
The title says 'Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model', but I'm struggling to reconcile this with the methodology. In standard RLHF (Section 2), we train a separate network $r_{	heta}$ to predict scores, then use PPO to update $ho_{policy}$. In DPO (Section 3), we seem to skip the reward model entirely and just minimize a binary cross-entropy loss on pairs $(y_w, y_l)$.

Specifically, look at Equation 7:
$$
abla_	heta 
abla 	ext{DPO} = ... - eta [ 
abla_	heta 	ext{log } ho(y_w | x) - 
abla_	heta 	ext{log } ho(y_l | x) ]$$
The text calls $	ilde{ho}(x,y) =  eta 	ext{log}  rac{ho(y|x)}{ho_{ref}(y|x)}$ an 'implicit reward'. But isn't this just saying that if I push up the probability of $y_w$ and down $y_l$, I am effectively maximizing that specific implicit reward? Why do we need to talk about 'rewards' at all if we aren't explicitly training a separate regressor? Is the distinction purely semantic, or is there a fundamental difference in what is being optimized compared to just doing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on $y_w$?

questions.title: Why does removing the importance weighting term cause model degeneration?
questions.question_body:
In Section 3 ('What does the DPO update do?'), the paper presents the gradient of the loss function. It highlights a specific term: $	ext{sigmoid}(	ilde{ho}(x, y_l) - 	ilde{ho}(x, y_w))$. The authors describe this as an 'importance weight' and mention that a 'naive version of this method without the weighting coefficient can cause the language model to degenerate.'

If I remove this sigmoid term from Equation 7, I get something that looks like standard unlikelihood training (pushing up $y_w$, pushing down $y_l$ with constant force). Why is this constant force bad? Intuitively, shouldn't we always want to push harder on examples where we are currently confident but wrong? Or perhaps push less when we are already right?

Could someone explain intuitively why multiplying by $	ext{sigmoid}(	ilde{ho}_{dispreferred} - 	ilde{ho}_{preferred})$ stabilizes training? What happens mathematically if $	ilde{ho}_{dispreferred}$ is extremely high?

questions.title: How does Theorem 1 guarantee no loss of generality regarding reward functions?
questions.question_body:
I am trying to understand Theorem 1 in Section 4. The theorem claims that 'all reward classes consistent with the Plackett-Luce models can be represented' by their reparameterization $r(x,y) =  eta 	ext{log}  rac{ho(y|x)}{ho_{ref}(y|x)}$.

The proof defines an equivalence relation where two rewards are equivalent if they differ only by a function of $x$, i.e., $r(x,y) - r'(x,y) = f(x)$. Lemma 1 says these equivalent rewards induce the same preference distribution. Okay.

But here is my confusion: Standard RLHF fits *any* reward function $r_	heta$. DPO restricts us to rewards that look like log-ratios of probabilities. Doesn't this restrict the space of possible reward functions we can learn? For example, if there exists a complex non-linear relationship between features and reward that cannot be expressed as $	ext{log}(ho/ho_{ref})$, wouldn't DPO fail to capture it?

The proof seems to rely on constructing *some* policy $ho_r$ from *any* given reward $r$. But in practice, our policy network has finite capacity (e.g., it's a Transformer). If our policy network cannot perfectly represent $ho_r$ derived from an arbitrary ground-truth reward, doesn't that mean we lose expressivity compared to fitting an explicit MLP-based reward model?

questions.title: Clarification on initialization when no SFT model is available
questions.question_body:
In Section 3 under 'DPO outline', the authors state: 'Since the preference datasets are sampled using $ho^{SFT}$, we initialize $ho_{ref} = ho^{SFT}$ whenever available.' However, they immediately follow with: 'when $ho^{SFT}$ is not available, we initialize $ho_{ref}$ by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions...'

Wait, isn't maximizing likelihood of preferred completions exactly what Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) *is*? So why distinguish between '$ho^{SFT}$' and '$ho_{ref}$ initialized by max likelihood'? Are they implying that sometimes you don't have an SFT checkpoint file saved from before you collected preferences?

Also, if you create your own reference policy by doing SFT on just the preferred data ($y_w$), isn't there now a massive distributional shift between your new $ho_{ref}$ and whatever policy originally generated those preferences? If humans labeled pairs generated by Model A (unknown), but you use Model B (trained on winners) as your reference for DPO equations like Eq. 7 ($	ext{log}( rac{	heta}{	ext{Ref}})$), won't this mismatch break the theoretical guarantee that DPO solves Eq. 6?

questions.title: Why does PPO require an extra baseline term while DPO does not?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4.2 ('Instability of Actor-Critic Algorithms'), Equation 9 shows an objective for PPO-like methods that includes a normalization term: $- eta 	ext{log} 	extstyle igcup_y ho_{ref}(y|x) e^{ rac{1}{ eta} r_	heta(x,y)}$. The authors call this a 'soft value function' or normalization term necessary for stability.

They argue that without this term (or approximating it poorly), gradients have high variance. However, in DPO (Eq. 7), there is absolutely no such summation over all possible outputs $y$. We only care about two specific tokens/sequences ($y_w$ and $y_l$).

How can DPO avoid needing this global normalization term entirely? Isn't maximizing relative log-probabilities without knowing how likely other sequences are risky? The paper suggests DPO yields a reward function where this term cancels out naturally due to parameterization. Could someone walk me through exactly how avoiding this summation changes the variance properties compared to standard PPO?
